title: Retting bast fibre for papermaking pulp
subtitle: Breaking down plant stems by water-retting to release the bast fibres for papermaking
excerpt: Bast fibres (the long fibres from the inner bark of plants like flax, hemp, stinging nettle, and kozo) make some of the strongest and longest-lived papers. Before they can be beaten into papermaking pulp, the fibres must be separated from the woody stem core. Water-retting does this by soaking the stems until bacterial and enzymatic action separates the fibre bundles.
sourceNotes: Dard Hunter, Papermaking: The History and Technique of an Ancient Craft (1943), chapters on Oriental papermaking fibres and on linen and hemp retting for Western handmade paper. Hunter describes water-retting as the traditional preparation for flax and hemp fibres in European and Japanese papermaking practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of soaking harvested plant stems in water (or laying them in damp fields) until bacteria and enzymes break down the pectin binding the bast fibre bundles to the woody core, making the fibres easy to separate.
Long cellulose fibres found in the inner bark (phloem) of plants including flax, hemp, jute, nettle, ramie, and mulberry (kozo). Bast fibres produce strong, long-fibred papers.
The woody inner core of a bast plant stem. After retting and breaking, the hurd separates from the bast fibre as short woody particles that must be removed before papermaking.

content.text: Retting is the oldest step in plant-fibre preparation, used in linen production for thousands of years before papermakers adopted the same fibres. In
for papermaking, the goal is to separate the long
so they can be beaten and formed into sheets. Under-retted fibres remain bound to the hurd and will not separate cleanly; over-retted fibres weaken and produce a lower-quality sheet.

Flax stalks (not seeds) and dried stinging nettle stems are the easiest bast fibres to source and ret in a domestic setting. Both produce a creamy-coloured, long-fibred pulp that forms sheets with good wet strength. Hemp gives a similar result but the stalks are woodier and require longer retting. Dry the stems fully before retting: green stems have a different fibre structure and ret unpredictably.

Bundle the dried stems loosely and submerge them in a bucket of water at room temperature or slightly warmer (18 to 24 degrees C). Weight them down with a stone or upturned plate so they remain submerged. Leave them to ret for 5 to 14 days. Check after 5 days by pulling one stem: if the bast fibres peel away from the hurd in long strips with gentle finger pressure, retting is complete. If the fibres resist, return the bundle to the water. Change the water once after 4 to 5 days if the smell becomes very strong: a mild fermentation smell is normal; a strongly putrid smell means the retting is proceeding too fast and the fibres may be weakening.

When the fibres test as fully retted, remove the bundle from the water and rinse thoroughly under running water. With both hands, break each stem over a firm edge (the side of a bucket or a rounded wooden block) to snap the hurd. The bast fibre will separate from the hurd fragments as long ribbons. Pull the ribbons away from the woody pieces and discard the hurd. Rinse the fibre ribbons again thoroughly. The washed fibres are now ready for cooking in a soda ash solution and then for beating.

items.symptom: After 14 days the fibres still will not separate from the hurd
items.cause: The water temperature was too low (below 15 degrees C), slowing bacterial action.
items.fix: Move the retting vessel to a warmer location, or add warm water daily to keep the temperature above 18 degrees C.

items.symptom: The retted fibres are very short and weak
items.cause: The stems sat in the water too long. Once the fibres separate easily, the bacteria keep working and start to break down the cellulose itself.
items.fix: Check the stems every day from day 5 onward. Once fibre separation is easy with light finger pressure, remove the stems immediately and rinse.
